en: So now that we understand what a REST API
generally is, let's design our API.
And if you listen carefully, you learned
that a REST API is defined by its API
endpoints, or at least that those API
endpoints are
an important part of a REST API.
Now here as an example, I want to build a
learning resources API. A simple API where
we can add, fetch, delete, and update
learning resources we wanna store. So for
example, a good course which we found, a
YouTube video, or simply a great blog
article.
So therefore, this API should have a couple
of endpoints.
We probably need one endpoint to fetch a
list of our resources that we stored.
And there, since we wanna fetch data, a GET
request makes sense, maybe to
/resources.
So ourdomain.com/resources,
and we don't attach any data to it because
it is just a GET request. We just wanna get
data.
Now, in order to get data, we also need to
store data. So we definitely also need an
endpoint for adding learning resources.
And since we want to add a new resource
every time and not override existing ones or
anything like that, this would be a POST
request to
/resources. That would make sense in my
opinion. And here we wanna attach some data
to the request. Let's say a learning
resource is made up by its title, its
description, its image URL, and a URL for
the resource itself.
The image URL is simply a little preview
image that we wanna display next to the
learning resource. And that's just my
definition of a learning resource here. Of
course, you could go with a different one.
Now we also want to be able to
edit or update a resource, so we need an
endpoint for that.
And it's up to you whether you wanna go with
PUT or PATCH.
I don't really wanna replace the existing
resource, I want to update it instead.
Hence, I'll go with a PATCH request to
/resources, but then
we'll also have a dynamic segment here to
have the ID of the resource as part of the
URL.
And then we can extract that ID on the
server side and we'll know which resource to
update. And there we also wanna attach some
data, the updated title, the updated
description,
updated image URL, URL, and so on.
Well, and last but not least, to complete
our CRUD operations,
we probably want to be able to delete a
resource and that would be a DELETE request
to
/resources/resource ID, where resource ID
again is dynamic
and we don't need to append any data to this
request. This will be the API I wanna build.
Now, before we build it, let's explore JSON
because that will be the data format which
we use for exchanging data.
